summary.short: Federal US statute criminalising knowing publication of nonconsensual intimate depictions, including AI-generated digital forgeries, and requiring covered online platforms to run notice-and-removal processes and remove reported depictions within 48 hours, enforced by the FTC; process set-up is due within one year of enactment.
summary.long: Amends Section 223 of the Communications Act of 1934 by inserting a new subsection (h). It makes unlawful the knowing publication, by any person using an interactive computer service in interstate or foreign commerce, of an authentic intimate visual depiction or a digital forgery (computer-generated, indistinguishable from an authentic depiction) of an identifiable individual without consent, where listed harm or intent conditions and exceptions apply. Publication involving adults is punishable by fine, up to 2 years' imprisonment, or both; involving minors, up to 3 years; threats to commit these offenses are also punishable. Courts must order forfeiture and restitution. Section 3 requires covered platforms to set up a notice-and-removal process within 1 year of enactment, post a plain-language notice, and remove a reported nonconsensual intimate depiction within 48 hours of a valid request, making reasonable efforts to remove known identical copies; good-faith removal is shielded from liability. The FTC enforces these duties as violations of a rule against unfair or deceptive practices. Section 4 defines covered platforms as public-facing websites or apps primarily hosting user-generated content or regularly publishing such depictions, excluding broadband access, email and preselected-content services.

relations.note: Sec. 2(a) redesignates subsection (h) as (i) and inserts a new subsection (h) on intentional disclosure of nonconsensual intimate visual depictions. Sec. 2(b) amends 47 U.S.C. 223(e)(1) and Sec. 2(c) amends subsection (i).
